test

1. Introduction

Modern AI systems are trained on an objective of striking narrowness: predict the next token, reconstruct a masked patch, minimise a loss on labelled examples. Yet the resulting systems behave, across a wide range of probes, as though they model the structure of the world that generated their data: spatial layouts, temporal order, physical regularities, other agents’ beliefs. This raises one of the central scientific questions of the field. How does a learning machine, given only samples from a world whose complexity vastly exceeds its own size, come to represent that world well enough to act on it?

There is no shortage of answers. Information theory says prediction is compression, and compression of data requires modelling its source (Shannon 1948; Solomonoff 1964; Delétang et al. 2024). Statistical learning theory points to the low intrinsic dimension of natural data (Pope et al. 2021; Sharma and Kaplan 2022). Scaling research describes smooth power-law improvement with size (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022) and explains it by the heavy-tailed structure of the world (Hutter 2021; Michaud et al. 2023). Mechanistic interpretability finds that networks store more concepts than they have dimensions by superposition (Elhage et al. 2022), and that they sometimes replace memorised look-up tables with compact algorithms (Power et al. 2022; Nanda et al. 2023). Work on in-context learning finds transformers performing something close to Bayesian inference over latent tasks at inference time (Xie et al. 2022; Garg et al. 2022). Critics, meanwhile, argue that learning from form alone cannot yield meaning (Bender and Koller 2020), and document characteristic failures — shortcut learning (Geirhos et al. 2020), incoherent implicit world models (Vafa et al. 2024), sensitivity to the statistics of the training task (McCoy et al. 2024).

These accounts are usually developed and tested in isolation, by different communities, on different systems. As a result it is unclear whether they compete, complement one another, or describe different levels of the same phenomenon. This paper attempts a comparative and integrative treatment. We do three things:

  1. Map the explanatory frameworks along eight dimensions — epistemic, information-theoretic, representational, geometric, statistical, mechanistic, inferential, and the limits — and state for each a testable core claim (Section 2).
  2. Build one controlled computational model per framework, in which the “world” is fully known, so that the claim can be checked against an exact theoretical reference rather than against intuition (Sections 3–4). The seven models are: a partially observable navigation world with an exact Bayes filter (E1); data manifolds of controlled intrinsic dimension (E2); a Zipf-distributed world of facts (E3); sparse features compressed through a bottleneck (E4); modular arithmetic (E5); in-context linear regression with controlled task diversity (E6); and a classification world with a planted spurious cue (E7).
  3. Synthesise the results into an account of what “understanding” amounts to for these systems, where each framework’s explanatory reach ends, and what would falsify the synthesis (Sections 5–6).

The contribution is not a new phenomenon — several of our experiments are deliberately minimal reproductions of known effects — but a common evidential standard applied across frameworks: every claim is tested against an analytically known optimum or a theoretically predicted exponent, with multiple seeds, untrained or randomised controls, and an explicit statement of what result would have counted against it. Everything runs on a CPU in a few hours from a single repository.

2. Explanatory frameworks: a multi-dimensional map

We organise the literature into eight dimensions. For each we give the core claim, the mechanism it posits, and the prediction we test. Table 1 summarises.

D1 — Epistemic: what would count as understanding? The debate over whether language models “understand” (Mitchell and Krakauer 2023) turns partly on definitions. The form-only critique (Bender and Koller 2020; Harnad 1990; Searle 1980) holds that a system trained on symbols alone cannot acquire meaning, because meaning is a relation between form and something outside it. A functionalist reading holds that a system understands a domain to the extent that it carries internal states that track the domain’s latent variables and that those states are used — causally — to produce appropriate behaviour, including under novel conditions. We adopt the functionalist criteria as operational tests without claiming they settle the philosophical question: (i) predictive adequacy relative to the optimum, (ii) recoverable latent structure, (iii) causal use of that structure, (iv) generalisation beyond the training distribution. Each experiment reports on whichever of these it can measure.

D2 — Information-theoretic: prediction as compression. By the source-coding theorem, minimising expected log-loss is minimising code length, and the minimum is achieved only by the true conditional distribution (Shannon 1948). Solomonoff induction and the MDL principle (Solomonoff 1964; Rissanen 1978; Hutter 2005) turn this into a theory of induction: the shortest description of data is the one that captures its generating process. The prediction: a sequence model trained on next-token loss should approach the entropy rate of the source, and closing the gap to the optimum should require representing the source’s hidden state, since that is the minimal sufficient statistic of the past for the future (Crutchfield and Young 1989; Shai et al. 2024). Neuroscience offers a parallel account in predictive coding (Rao and Ballard 1999; Friston 2010; Clark 2013).

D3 — Representational: emergent world models. Models trained only on move sequences in Othello represent the board state, recoverably and causally (Li et al. 2023; Nanda, Lee, and Wattenberg 2023); LLMs carry linear representations of geographic and temporal coordinates (Gurnee and Tegmark 2024); transformers trained on hidden Markov processes linearly embed the Bayesian belief simplex (Shai et al. 2024). The linear representation hypothesis (Park, Choe, and Veitch 2024; Mikolov, Yih, and Zweig 2013) and the convergence of representations across models (Huh et al. 2024) generalise the point. Sceptics note that probes can find structure that the model does not use (Hewitt and Liang 2019; Belinkov 2022), and that implicit world models can pass standard diagnostics while being incoherent (Vafa et al. 2024). The prediction: latent state should be linearly decodable well above an untrained control, and interventions on the decoded representation should change predictions as the world model implies.

D4 — Geometric: the manifold hypothesis. High-dimensional observations of the world are generated by comparatively few factors, so they concentrate near low-dimensional manifolds (Pope et al. 2021; Ansuini et al. 2019; Facco et al. 2017). Nonparametric learning in d dimensions requires sample sizes exponential in d, so the curse of dimensionality is governed by intrinsic, not ambient, dimension, and power-law learning-curve exponents should scale as 1/d (Sharma and Kaplan 2022; Bahri et al. 2024). Symmetry and locality priors further reduce the effective dimension (Bronstein et al. 2021; Lin, Tegmark, and Rolnick 2017). The prediction: learning-curve exponents depend on d and are insensitive to ambient dimension D.

D5 — Statistical: scaling laws and a heavy-tailed world. Loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022). One explanation is that the world consists of many discrete regularities (“quanta”) whose usefulness is Zipf-distributed (Zipf 1949); a capacity-limited learner acquires them in order of frequency, so the exponent is inherited from the world’s frequency distribution (Michaud et al. 2023; Hutter 2021). The prediction: for frequency exponent α, error scales as N^−(α−1) in capacity and D^−(α−1)/α in data.

D6 — Mechanistic: superposition and compact algorithms. Two mechanisms let a bounded network represent an unbounded-seeming world. Superposition: when features are sparse, a network can store many more of them than it has dimensions, as nearly orthogonal directions, at the cost of interference (Elhage et al. 2022; Bricken et al. 2023; Templeton et al. 2024). Algorithmic compression: networks can move from memorising examples to implementing a rule — in modular addition, a Fourier-basis “clock” algorithm — and do so abruptly (“grokking”) under a pressure toward simplicity such as weight decay (Power et al. 2022; Nanda et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2022; Gromov 2023). Both connect to the broader evidence that deep networks are biased toward simple functions (Valle-Pérez, Camargo, and Louis 2019; Goldblum et al. 2024), which is what makes generalisation possible despite their capacity to memorise (Zhang et al. 2017; Wolpert 1996). Predictions: superposition grows with feature sparsity and is absent in linear models; generalisation on algorithmic tasks coincides with the emergence of a structured, low-norm representation.

D7 — Inferential: in-context Bayesian inference. Pre-trained transformers adapt to new tasks from examples in their context, without weight updates (Garg et al. 2022; Olsson et al. 2022). On this view, pre-training over a distribution of “worlds” amortises Bayesian inference: the network learns a prior and an inference procedure, and the context supplies the evidence (Xie et al. 2022); mechanistic accounts implement this with gradient-descent-like updates in the forward pass (Oswald et al. 2023; Akyürek et al. 2023). Raventós et al. (2023) showed that the prior the network learns depends on the diversity of pre-training worlds: below a threshold it is Bayes-optimal for the finite pool it saw, and above it, it generalises to new worlds. The prediction: with high diversity the model tracks the Bayes-optimal ridge estimator on unseen worlds; with low diversity it tracks the pool-restricted Bayes estimator and fails on unseen worlds.

D8 — Limits: shortcuts, simplicity bias and distribution shift. The same biases that enable generalisation produce characteristic failures. A network will use whatever predictive cue is simplest to extract, including spurious ones (Geirhos et al. 2020; Shah et al. 2020), and robust behaviour requires that the data — or the training objective — break the spurious correlation (Sagawa et al. 2020; Schölkopf et al. 2021). Compositional and systematic generalisation remain fragile (B. Lake and Baroni 2018; Dziri et al. 2023; B. M. Lake et al. 2017). The prediction: reliance on a spurious cue grows with its training correlation, can dominate even when the true cue is perfectly predictive, and is removed by interventions that decorrelate the cue.

3. Methods: seven model worlds

Every experiment uses a world whose generating process we control, so that each framework’s claim can be scored against an exact or theoretically derived reference. All models are trained from scratch in JAX on a 4-core CPU. Exact configurations are in the code (wu/e*.py); the main choices are given here. Unless noted, results are means over three seeds with ±1 s.d.

E1 — Partially observable navigation (D1, D2, D3). An agent occupies one of the free cells of a 6×6 grid with six obstacle cells, facing one of four headings: S = 120 hidden states. Each free cell carries one of three colours, so local views are heavily aliased. A trajectory is a token sequence BOS o₀ a₁ o₁ … a₂₀ o₂₀, where each action aₜ ∈ {Forward, Left, Right} is uniform-random and each observation oₜ is the colour of the cell directly ahead of the agent, or wall. The model is never told that a grid, position or heading exist. Because the world is a hidden Markov model with deterministic dynamics, the Bayes-optimal predictor is computable exactly by forward filtering over the 120 states; its log-loss is the entropy rate of the observation process, the floor that no predictor can beat. As surface-statistics baselines we fit back-off n-gram models (n = 1…12) on 200,000 trajectories — ten times more sequences than the transformer sees in training — and report the best. The learner is a 4-layer, 64-dimensional, 4-head pre-LayerNorm transformer trained for 5,000 steps (batch 64) on next-token loss over the whole sequence.

We evaluate four things. Compression: log-loss on observation tokens against the Bayes floor and the n-gram baseline. Representation: multinomial logistic-regression probes, trained on 70% of 3,000 held-out trajectories and tested on the rest, decode the true state (120-way), cell (30-way) and heading (4-way) from the residual stream at each layer, at the action positions from which the next observation is predicted. Because the state is sometimes genuinely ambiguous, the relevant ceiling is the accuracy of the Bayes-filter MAP state, not 100%. An identically shaped untrained network serves as the control for probe expressivity (Hewitt and Liang 2019). Causality: for test positions where the Bayes belief has collapsed (max > 0.99) onto a state A, we add μ_B − μ_A to the residual stream at layer ℓ, where μ_s is the mean training residual for state s, choosing a target state B whose view differs from A’s. We then rerun the remaining layers and ask whether the model now predicts B’s view. Controls are a random direction of equal norm and no patch. Robustness: the action policy is shifted at test time (P(Forward) = 0.7 rather than 1/3), which changes trajectory statistics but not the world. We also record the representational similarity (Spearman ρ) between the distances of cell-mean representations and grid Manhattan distances, TwoNN intrinsic dimension (Facco et al. 2017) per layer, and probe accuracy over training.

E2 — Data manifolds of controlled dimension (D4). Latents z ∈ [0,1]^d (d ∈ {2,3,4,6,8}) are mapped to observations x ∈ ℝ⁶⁴ by a fixed random two-layer tanh network. The target y = Σⱼ aⱼ cos(2π ωⱼ·z + φⱼ) has 32 random Fourier components, with ωⱼ ~ N(0, (1.5²/d) I), so that the function’s variation along any direction is matched across d. A two-hidden-layer MLP (width 256) is trained on n ∈ {2⁷,…,2¹⁴} samples with early stopping on a validation set, and normalised test MSE (MSE / Var y) is recorded. We fit the learning-curve exponent and test whether it scales as c/d. As a control, d = 4 latents are embedded into D ∈ {16, 64, 256} ambient dimensions. TwoNN is applied to the synthetic data and to the 8×8 handwritten digits (Pope et al. 2021).

E3 — A Zipfian world of facts (D5). The world contains K = 2,048 facts: random input vectors xₖ ∈ ℝ³² with random labels yₖ ∈ {1…32}, encountered with probability pₖ ∝ k^−α, α ∈ {1.5, 2.0, 2.5}. Labels are random, so no fact can be inferred from another; the only route to low error is storage. Capacity scaling: one-hidden-layer MLPs with 4–256 hidden units (N = 292 to 16,672 parameters) minimise the expected (p-weighted) loss — the infinite-data limit — for 6,000 full-batch Adam steps. Data scaling: a width-256 MLP is trained to convergence on the empirical distribution of D ∈ {2⁸,…,2¹⁶} draws. The metric is the p-weighted error rate. Theory (Section 2, D5) predicts slopes −(α−1) and −(α−1)/α respectively. We also compute the exact finite-K “unseen mass” curve Σₖ pₖ(1−pₖ)^D (1 − 1/32).

E4 — Superposition (D6). Following Elhage et al. (2022), n = 20 features xᵢ ~ U[0,1], each zero with probability S, are encoded as h = Wx ∈ ℝ⁵ and decoded as x̂ = ReLU(Wᵀh + b), with importance-weighted MSE (Iᵢ = 0.85^i). We sweep S from 0 to 0.997 and compare a linear decoder. A feature counts as represented if ‖Wᵢ‖ > 0.5. A second sweep with n = 100, m = 10 and uniform importance measures features stored per dimension.

E5 — Modular arithmetic (D6). The task is a + b mod 97, with 30% of the 9,409 pairs used for training. The model is a learned 128-d embedding followed by a 256-unit ReLU layer, trained full-batch with AdamW (lr 10⁻³, β₂ = 0.98) for 20,000 steps. We sweep weight decay ∈ {0, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3} and training fraction ∈ {0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.7}. Fourier concentration is the share of (mean-removed) embedding power in the top 6 of 48 discrete Fourier frequencies; uniform spreading would give 0.125.

E6 — In-context inference over worlds (D7). Each sequence (x₁,y₁,…,x₁₆,y₁₆) is drawn from its own linear world, y = w·x + ε, with x, w ∈ ℝ⁵, w ~ N(0, I) and ε ~ N(0, 0.25²). A 4-layer, 64-d transformer predicts each yᵢ from the preceding pairs. Pre-training task diversity is either a fixed pool of M ∈ {8, 64, 512, 4096} worlds or unlimited (fresh w per sequence). References are ridge regression with λ = σ² (the Bayes posterior mean under the Gaussian prior), least squares, and dMMSE (the Bayes posterior mean under a uniform prior over the M pool worlds) (Raventós et al. 2023). We evaluate on unseen worlds and measure the mean squared distance between the model’s predictions and each estimator’s.

E7 — A world with a planted shortcut (D8). On 8×8 digits, the task is digit ≥ 5. A 2×2 “watermark” is placed top-left for one class and top-right for the other, agreeing with the label for a fraction ρ of training images. An MLP (64-128-2) is trained on 60% of the data (5 seeds) and tested on held-out images with the watermark agreeing, absent, or reversed. At ρ = 0.95 we compare standard training with two remedies: group-balanced reweighting (Sagawa et al. 2020) and randomising the watermark, an intervention that cuts its causal link to the label.

Evidential standard. For each experiment we specify in advance the outcome that would count against the framework’s prediction (Table 2), report all conditions run, and give the untrained, random-direction or linear-model control. Code, configurations, raw results (JSON) and figure scripts are released together, and the full pipeline runs in a few CPU-hours.

4.2 E2 — Complexity lives in the intrinsic, not the ambient, dimension

Intrinsic dimension is recoverable from samples alone. TwoNN returns 2.04 ± 0.03, 2.89 ± 0.03, 3.94 ± 0.05, 5.61 ± 0.04 and 7.33 ± 0.10 for d = 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 (Fig. E2c). Embedding the same d = 4 manifold in 16, 64 or 256 ambient dimensions leaves the estimate unchanged (3.93, 3.88, 3.87). The mild underestimate at d = 8 is the known negative bias of nearest-neighbour estimators at higher d with a few thousand points (Facco et al. 2017). The 64-pixel handwritten digits have a TwoNN dimension of 8.9, and 21 principal components are needed for 90% of their variance — consistent with prior reports that natural images are far lower-dimensional than their pixel count (Pope et al. 2021).

Sample efficiency is governed by d, as theory predicts. Errors at a fixed sample size rise steeply with d (Fig. E2a). At n = 16,384, normalised test MSE is 8×10⁻⁵ for d = 2 and 0.18 for d = 8. The samples needed to reach normalised error 0.1 grow from about 160 (d = 3) to 550 (d = 4) to 5,900 (d = 6), and d = 8 does not reach it within the budget. Fitting e(n) = a·n^−β + f per seed gives exponents β that fall as 1/d: a one-parameter fit β = c/d explains 96% of the variance across d, with c = 4.9 (Fig. E2b). Sharma & Kaplan’s (2022) argument for piecewise-linear networks predicts β ≈ 4/d for squared loss. Our estimate is of the same form and magnitude, slightly steeper, as expected for a smooth (band-limited) target. The ambient-dimension control gives near-identical naive slopes for D = 16, 64 and 256 (−0.97, −1.08, −1.09).

Two caveats. The naive whole-curve log–log slope does not reproduce the 1/d law (R² = 0.18), because the low-d curves saturate at an optimisation floor and the d = 8 curve has not yet reached its asymptotic regime. The c/d result therefore depends on modelling the floor explicitly. And at d = 8 the fitted β·d is about 3, below the others (about 5), consistent with a pre-asymptotic curve still bending downward. We report both fits.

Interpretation. A complex-looking world is learnable to the extent that its variation is generated by few factors. The curse of dimensionality is real, but it is indexed by intrinsic dimension, and learning curves carry its signature in their exponent. This is a precondition for D5: power-law scaling with an exponent set by the data.

4.3 E3 — Scaling exponents are inherited from the world’s frequency distribution

Data scaling matches theory quantitatively. With enough capacity to memorise everything it sees, a model’s error is the probability mass of facts it has not yet seen. The fitted exponents are −0.52 for α = 2 (asymptotic theory −0.50) and −0.60 for α = 2.5 (theory −0.60), with R² ≥ 0.99 (Fig. E3b). For α = 1.5 the fit (−0.48) is steeper than the asymptotic −0.33, but it matches the exact finite-K curve (−0.50): with K = 2,048 facts, the heavy tail is truncated within our data range. Across all three α the measured error lies on the exact unseen-mass curve. The exponent of the data-scaling law is therefore a property of the world, not of the network.

Capacity scaling is ordered by frequency but not purely capacity-limited. Models learn facts in rank order (Fig. E3c). Each larger model extends a solid block of learned facts to rarer ranks, and its error is within 1.2–1.6× of the ideal “learn the top-n facts” error for the larger models (2–12× for the smallest). Capacity-scaling exponents are −0.94, −0.84 and −1.08 for α = 1.5, 2.0 and 2.5, against the quantization-model predictions of −0.5, −1.0 and −1.5. They do not track α as the theory predicts. The reason is visible in the number of facts learned, which grows as N^0.78, N^0.49 and N^0.35 rather than linearly in N. For α = 2.5, the largest network learns only 330 facts, although the same architecture learns 2,018 when α = 1.5. Rare facts receive gradient in proportion to their frequency, so within a fixed optimisation budget the effective number of stored quanta is set by optimisation as much as by capacity (for α = 1.5 the curve also steepens as n approaches K).

Interpretation. The quantization picture — a world made of many discrete regularities, acquired in order of usefulness — survives as a mechanism: we observe frequency-ordered acquisition directly. Its simplest quantitative form (stored quanta ∝ parameters) does not hold in our compute-limited regime. This is a real distinction, not a technicality: in practice the variable that sets an exponent can be compute rather than parameters (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022), and an exponent measured in one regime should not be read as a property of the world without knowing which resource bound it.

4.4 E4 — Superposition lets a small network hold a large, sparse world

With dense features, the ReLU model behaves exactly like a linear one: it represents the 5 most important features orthogonally and drops the other 15 (Fig. E4a,b). As features become sparse, the number represented rises past the number of dimensions: 10 at S = 0.75, 15 at S = 0.97, and 18.7 ± 1.2 of 20 at S = 0.997. They are packed as non-orthogonal directions (Fig. E4c), with mean interference Σⱼ≠ᵢ(Ŵᵢ·Wⱼ)² rising from 0 to 3.5, and dimensions per feature falling from 1.0 to 0.21. The linear model never represents more than 5 features at any sparsity. At S = 0.997 the ReLU model’s loss is 5× lower (5×10⁻⁴ against 2.7×10⁻³). In the larger setting (n = 100, m = 10), features stored per dimension climb from below 1 (dense) through 4.3 (S = 0.9) to 9.8–10 (S ≥ 0.98), where effectively every feature is stored (Fig. E4d). The low dense-regime value reflects equal importances, which let the model spread small weights below our representation threshold.

Interpretation. Real-world concepts are sparse: any scene or sentence involves a tiny fraction of the concepts a system knows. E4 reproduces the result of Elhage et al. (2022) that this sparsity lets a bounded network represent many more concepts than it has dimensions, at the price of interference. Interference is negligible when features rarely co-occur, and it is filtered by the nonlinearity. The capacity puzzle — how a network with d dimensions can know millions of things — has a concrete answer, and it predicts that the units of knowledge are directions rather than neurons (Bricken et al. 2023; Templeton et al. 2024).

4.7 E7 — The limits: the network learns the simplest predictive cue, not the intended one

When the watermark is uninformative (ρ = 0.5), the network ignores it: accuracy is 98% whether the watermark agrees with the label or is reversed. As ρ rises, accuracy on reversed-watermark images falls monotonically: 96% (ρ = 0.75), 87% (0.9), 74% (0.95), 22% (0.99) and 0% (ρ = 1). Accuracy on unmarked images falls too, from 96% to 74% (Fig. E7a). The striking case is ρ = 1, where both cues predict the label perfectly. The network trains to 100% accuracy and relies on the watermark almost exclusively, although the digit shape it was meant to learn would have generalised. On watermark-only images (a blank digit with the patch) it scores 100% for every ρ ≥ 0.9. This is simplicity bias (Shah et al. 2020): a single corner patch is linearly separable with a large margin, and the network’s inductive bias favours it.

Of the remedies (Fig. E7b), group-balanced reweighting raises reversed-watermark accuracy only from 74% to 80% at ρ = 0.95. With 5% minority examples, the model can still fit the majority shortcut and memorise the exceptions. Randomising the watermark — an intervention that severs its causal relation to the label — restores reversed-watermark accuracy to 98% and unmarked accuracy to 96%, matching a model never shown a watermark (98%).

Interpretation. E7 is the counterweight to E1–E6. Every mechanism that lets a network compress a world — preferring simple, low-norm, high-margin explanations — will also seize on any simple regularity that happens to predict the target, whether or not it reflects the world’s causal structure. Prediction rewards correlation, not cause. The only reliable fix in our experiment is to change the data so that the shortcut stops working: an intervention, not more data from the same distribution (Schölkopf et al. 2021; Geirhos et al. 2020).
